items.explanation: Each instinct guards one danger, and one short prepared conversation guards both. A middle-length list still improvises reasons.
items.reference:
Two instincts, one answer
over-explain: protects dignity, risks the record
under-explain: protects safety, feels cold
short, factual, prepared: serves both
Why: clarity, brevity and respect are humane and sound at once, so the trade-off is false.
items.learnMore:
Kind and safe point the same way

Over- and under-explaining each guard one danger. A short, factual, prepared conversation guards both, because it neither improvises reasons nor sounds cold.

Common mistake

Picking one instinct and assuming the other cost is unavoidable.
items.reflection: Think of a hard message you gave or received. Did it feel kind because of what was said, or because of how clear it was?

choices: Answer from memory so that he looks fully prepared to everyone
Promise to find out and decide the answer later on his own
Hand the question to the HR colleague; specifics are not his to answer
End the meeting immediately so that no mistake can be made in it
items.explanation: A second person exists for questions outside the manager's role.
items.reference:
Ready before walking in
📅 last working day: exact date
💶 pay and benefits: owed and when written details follow
🔑 access and equipment: when and how
🧑‍💼 second person: confirmed in the room
Why: the first three are facts to state; the fourth is a safeguard for the process.
items.learnMore:
Prepare the preparable

Practical details are the easiest part to prepare fully and the worst to improvise. A second person witnesses the talk and answers questions that are not the manager's to answer.

Common mistake

Winging pay, benefits or equipment details because the reason felt like the hard part.

items.prompt: What is the first response to 'this isn't fair'?
choices: Defend it
Leave the room without saying anything more
Acknowledge the feeling

items.prompt: What does the manager restate?
choices: The written basis
A new reason that was raised just now
The person's whole history, week by week

items.prompt: What does the manager decline to do?
choices: Answer any question put to him there
Re-argue the decision
Care about how the person feels at all today

items.prompt: Where does the manager turn next?
choices: To a longer debate
To a vote
To what comes next

items.prompt: Why not defend the plan's fairness at length?
choices: Fairness was settled in the plan, so it is not reopened in the room
It is rude to speak
It takes too much room

items.prompt: What if the objection comes up again?
choices: Argue louder
The same calm answer, once more
Add a brand new reason to prove the point

items.prompt: Which behaviour makes the meeting adversarial?
choices: Calm restating of the written reason
Having an HR colleague present in the room
Matching frustration with frustration

items.prompt: What does the flat zero of new reasons mean?
choices: No new reasons were added
Nothing at all was said during the meeting
The meeting was cancelled before it started

items.prompt: Elena says for the second time she was never given a real chance, and Marcus wants to prove otherwise. What does the unit advise?
choices: Prove it with a detailed history of each single week of the plan
Repeat the acknowledgment and written basis briefly, then move on
Concede that the plan was unfair and reconsider the decision at once
Raise his voice so that the point finally lands very clearly
items.explanation: A second defense is the moment most likely to produce an off-record reason.
items.reference:
When Elena objects
acknowledge: 'I hear this feels unfair'
restate once: the written plan and June 30
decline to re-argue
turn to next steps with the HR colleague
Why: a second, louder defense turns a clean meeting adversarial.
items.learnMore:
Same words, calmly

Acknowledge, restate the written basis once, decline to re-argue, and turn to next steps. A repeated objection gets the same calm answer, not a new justification.

Common mistake

Defending the plan at length, or matching the person's frustration.
